purpose: Per-machine hold rules. A hold is scored differently depending on whether the muscle is still loaded in that position or the load has been taken off it. Without this every pause is judged the same way, which penalises a client for holding a loaded contraction and lets a rest at the bottom pass.
classificationTest: Put the machine in the hold position and ask: if the client completely relaxed right now, would the stack move? If it drops, the muscle was holding it -> LOADED. If nothing happens, the skeleton or the resting plates are taking the load -> REST.

rules.LOADED: The hold is work. Scored one-sided, like a contraction: cutting it short deducts, holding longer than target is free and keeps full marks. Decided deliberately — a client holding 6s against a 2s target scores 100, and a set can run long without costing quality marks as long as nothing is rushed. Accepted because the muscle is under load throughout.
rules.REST: The hold is dead time. Scored both ways: cutting it short deducts, and so does running long, since tension is off and the extra seconds are rest rather than work.
rules.shortAlwaysDeducts: Cutting any hold short deducts, on every machine and at both ends. The classification only decides whether running LONG costs anything.

positions.top: Stack raised. Always the end of the concentric and the muscle at its shortest, whichever way the client's limb travelled.
positions.bottom: Stack down. Start position, muscle at its longest. Coached as a HOVER throughout, so the plates stay off the stack and the muscle keeps holding the load — LOADED by default. Setting the plates down would release tension and make it REST.

machines.name: Hip Extension
machines.notes: Single joint at the hip. The top was the doubtful end, because a hip extension machine could reach a stop at full extension the way B6 Leg Press reaches a knee lockout, which would shed the load and make it REST. Confirmed by the coach on 20 October that the stack would drop if the client relaxed there, so the top is LOADED and a long hold at full extension is work rather than rest. Bottom is LOADED by the coached-hover policy. Worked with both legs.

machines.name: Hip Abduction
machines.notes: Legs driven apart against the pads. Nothing skeletal can take over at full abduction: relax and the stack pulls the legs back together, so the top is LOADED. Bottom is LOADED by the coached-hover policy. Worked with both legs.

machines.name: Hip Adduction
machines.notes: Legs squeezed together against the pads. Confirmed by the coach on 24 October: the top is LOADED. The load pulls the legs apart, so a relaxed client loses the position and the stack drops. The lever does not reach a hard stop before the legs meet, which was the one way this could have been REST. Bottom is LOADED by the coached-hover policy. Worked with both legs.

machines.name: Leg Extension
machines.notes: Knee cannot lock out and shed load to the skeleton, so the quad holds the leg against the pad through full extension. Bottom is a coached hover, so the quad keeps holding the load in the stretched position.

machines.name: Leg Curl
machines.notes: Hamstring holds the pad against resistance at full knee flexion, with no position the skeleton can take over. Bottom is a coached hover, so the hamstring keeps holding the load in the stretched position.

machines.name: Leg Curl (seated)
machines.notes: Hamstring holds against resistance at full flexion. Bottom confirmed LOADED by the coach: this machine keeps tension at both ends, so the submitted REST was wrong and the coached-hover policy was right. No longer an open question.

machines.name: Tibialis Dorsi Flexion
machines.notes: Bottom set to LOADED by the coached-hover policy. Small joint through a small range, so stack travel is likely to be the shortest in the estate — tape it and check the signal ratio before relying on this one. May only be viable at a quicker tempo.

machines.name: Leg Press
machines.notes: First machine where the two ends differ. At the top the knees lock and the load passes through the skeleton, so holding there is rest however it is coached — the hover policy does not override it. At the bottom the knees are flexed and the quads hold the carriage, so the hover is work. Often geared 2:1 to keep the stack manageable, which would halve the travel the phone sees — worth taping. The lockout reasoning here was reviewed and accepted by the coach on 24 October, alongside the D6 check. That is weaker than A1's confirmation, which came from putting the machine in the hold position and testing it: this one is agreement that a locked knee or elbow obviously sheds the load, not an observation of this machine's stack.

machines.name: Chest Press
machines.notes: Confirmed by the coach on 24 October: at the finish the elbows lock out and the load passes through the skeleton, so the hold there is rest however it is coached. The doubt that prompted the check was the converging handle path - the handles travel toward the midline as well as forward, which resembles D5 Arm Cross, where limbs meeting rather than a joint locking is what ends the movement. On this machine the press reaches extension, so the lockout argument holds and the resemblance is superficial. Bottom is a coached hover and stays loaded.

machines.name: Seated Dip
machines.notes: Same rules as B6 Leg Press: elbows lock out at the top and the load passes through the skeleton, so the hold there is rest however it is coached. Bottom is a coached hover and stays loaded. The lockout reasoning here was reviewed and accepted by the coach on 24 October, alongside the D6 check. That is weaker than A1's confirmation, which came from putting the machine in the hold position and testing it: this one is agreement that a locked knee or elbow obviously sheds the load, not an observation of this machine's stack.

machines.name: Arm Cross
machines.notes: Arms brought together across the chest. Confirmed by the coach on 24 October: the top is LOADED. The load pulls the arms apart, so relaxing loses the position, and the levers do not reach a stop that would take the load first. This is the contrast that made D6 Chest Press worth re-checking the same day. Both movements bring the handles toward the midline, and they differ only because the press also reaches elbow extension and sheds the load to the skeleton, while this one ends with the arms meeting under tension. A converging path is not a lockout. Bottom is LOADED by the coached-hover policy. Worked with both arms.

machines.name: Overhead Press (front grip)
machines.notes: Same rules as B6 Leg Press: elbows lock out at the top and the load passes through the skeleton, so the hold there is rest however it is coached. Bottom is a coached hover and stays loaded. One physical machine with two grips, recorded as separate codes so each keys cleanly and can carry its own travel. Grip-to-code mapping taken as front=E3, rear=E1 — swap if that is the wrong way round. The lockout reasoning here was reviewed and accepted by the coach on 24 October, alongside the D6 check. That is weaker than A1's confirmation, which came from putting the machine in the hold position and testing it: this one is agreement that a locked knee or elbow obviously sheds the load, not an observation of this machine's stack.

machines.name: Overhead Press (rear grip)
machines.notes: Same rules as B6 Leg Press: elbows lock out at the top and the load passes through the skeleton, so the hold there is rest however it is coached. Bottom is a coached hover and stays loaded. One physical machine with two grips, recorded as separate codes so each keys cleanly and can carry its own travel. Grip-to-code mapping taken as front=E3, rear=E1 — swap if that is the wrong way round. The lockout reasoning here was reviewed and accepted by the coach on 24 October, alongside the D6 check. That is weaker than A1's confirmation, which came from putting the machine in the hold position and testing it: this one is agreement that a locked knee or elbow obviously sheds the load, not an observation of this machine's stack.

machines.name: Lateral Raise
machines.notes: Shoulder abduction against the pads. The deltoid carries the load through the whole range and there is no lockout at the top, unlike the overhead presses E1 and E3. Bottom is LOADED by the coached-hover policy.

machines.name: Internal Rotation (humerus)
machines.notes: Single joint at the shoulder, rotating the humerus. There is no position in the range where the joint locks out and passes the load to the frame, so both ends are LOADED by the same rule as the other single-joint machines. Worked one arm at a time, and left and right are kept apart because they are different work and an imbalance between them is the thing most worth seeing on a rotation machine. Rotator-cuff machines move the stack a short way, so this is a likely candidate for the short-stroke limit: tape the maximum early. The app will say per set whether the stroke can carry the prescribed tempo, and at 4-2-4-2 that needs roughly 160mm.

machines.name: External Rotation (humerus)
machines.notes: Single joint at the shoulder, rotating the humerus. There is no position in the range where the joint locks out and passes the load to the frame, so both ends are LOADED by the same rule as the other single-joint machines. Worked one arm at a time, and left and right are kept apart because they are different work and an imbalance between them is the thing most worth seeing on a rotation machine. Rotator-cuff machines move the stack a short way, so this is a likely candidate for the short-stroke limit: tape the maximum early. The app will say per set whether the stroke can carry the prescribed tempo, and at 4-2-4-2 that needs roughly 160mm.

machines.name: Pullover
machines.notes: Single joint, confirmed by the coach as carrying the same loaded profile as B7: the muscle holds the load at both ends and no position lets the frame or the skeleton take it. Recorded here because the first classification reached the right answer by the wrong route — it was filed with the multi-joint pulls on the push/pull rule, when it belongs with the single-joint machines, which have no lockout available to them at all.

machines.name: Row
machines.notes: Multi-joint but a PULL, so there is no lockout: the stack-up position is the most challenging point of the movement, with the back holding the handle in against the load. Confirmed by the coach. LOADED despite sharing a joint count with the pressing machines, which is why the divide is push versus pull. Often geared 2:1, which would halve the travel the phone sees. Confirmed by the coach as workable one side at a time, so left and right are recorded separately.

machines.name: Pulldown
machines.notes: Multi-joint but a PULL, so there is no lockout: the stack-up position is the most challenging point of the movement, with the back holding the handle in against the load. Confirmed by the coach. LOADED despite sharing a joint count with the pressing machines, which is why the divide is push versus pull. Often geared 2:1, which would halve the travel the phone sees. Confirmed by the coach as workable one side at a time, so left and right are recorded separately.

machines.name: Torso Arm (supinated grip)
machines.notes: Pulling movement with the elbow flexing, supinated grip. No lockout anywhere in the range, so the lats and arm hold the stack at the top of the contraction. Bottom is LOADED by the coached-hover policy.

machines.name: Torso Row
machines.notes: Pulling movement. The elbow cannot lock out into a position that sheds the load, so the top of the contraction is held by the muscle. Same classification as C7 Row. Bottom is LOADED by the coached-hover policy. Worked with both arms.

machines.name: Trunk Rotation
machines.notes: Single joint through the spine, rotation rather than flexion, so it is classified with F2.1 and the other single-joint machines: no position where a limb can lock out, so the top is LOADED. The bottom was the doubtful one — a rotation machine can have a pad or a stop at square that takes the load, which would make it REST, and F2.1's confirmation was about a seat back on a flexion machine and did not carry across. Confirmed by the coach on 16 October as LOADED at both ends, so the hover policy stands here too and either end may be held as long as the client likes. Worked one side at a time, and left and right are recorded separately because rotation to each side is different work and averaging them would hide the asymmetry that is the point of measuring it.

machines.name: Trunk Flexion
machines.notes: Single joint through the spine, no position where a limb can lock out, so the top hold is LOADED by the same reasoning as the other single-joint machines. The START position was the doubtful one: on some trunk flexion machines the client sits back against the frame at full extension and the stack rests there, which would shed the load and make the bottom REST. Confirmed by the coach on 16 October that the stack would drop if the client relaxed at the upright start, so the bottom is LOADED too and both ends may be held as long as the client likes. A set recorded on this machine on 8 October ran 20 of 23 turnarounds with no pause at all, so neither hold has yet been observed held.

machines.name: Shrug
machines.notes: Single joint, scapular elevation. Nothing bony stops the scapula rising, so there is no lockout at the top and the traps hold the stack there: LOADED. Bottom is LOADED by the coached-hover policy and by the classification test as it is written — with the plates held off, a client who relaxed completely would drop the stack. Worth a second look all the same: at full depression a shrug hangs partly on passive structures rather than on working muscle, which is a finer distinction than "would the stack move" can catch, and if the coach wants the bottom treated as rest this is the machine to say so about. Recorded as bilateral because nothing has been said otherwise. Likely short in the stack: scapular elevation covers little distance, so like B8 and the two rotation machines this is a candidate for the short-stroke limit and worth taping early.

machines.name: Neck Extension
machines.notes: Single joint through the cervical spine. There is no position where the skeleton can take the load off the neck extensors, so the top is LOADED by the same rule as the other single-joint machines, and the bottom is LOADED by the coached-hover policy. Classified by that rule rather than confirmed one machine at a time, as B5, B8, C7 and C3 were. OUT OF THE MEASUREMENT ENVELOPE as things stand: a set recorded on it read 18-23mm a stroke and was refused outright for moving less than the 100mm floor, the app naming the reason as "stack moved only 19mm per rep". That figure is one client's stroke, not the machine's hard-stop maximum, so the maximum is still worth taping — but at a fifth of the floor it would have to be far larger than anything observed for this machine to come back in, and the hold classification is moot until it does.

machines.name: Curl
machines.notes: Single joint through the elbow, confirmed by the coach as the machine behind the 21:19 set on 16 October. Same loaded profile as B7 and C1: at full flexion there is no position where the skeleton can take the load, so the top is LOADED, and the bottom is a coached hover and stays loaded too. Stroke measured about 280mm from the four strokes in that recording that read cleanly, which is ample for the estate tempo — an earlier reading of 107mm was the median of a set whose strokes were splitting, not the machine. Worked one arm at a time, confirmed by the coach, so left and right are recorded separately. The 21:19 set on 16 October was performed with both arms, so the absent side on that record is correct rather than missing: bilateral is the ordinary case and carries no side, on this machine as on every other that can be worked one side at a time.

coaching.note: Clients are always coached to hover at the bottom rather than set the plates down. A hovered stack stays suspended, so the muscle is still holding it and the bottom hold is LOADED by default across the estate. A machine only overrides this if its own bottom position genuinely sheds the load.

notes: What decides the top hold is whether the movement ends at a joint lockout. A press reaches extension and the skeleton takes the load, so its top hold is REST. Everything else holds the load in the muscle and is LOADED at the top, however many joints are involved: pulls, which have no lockout available, and the movements that finish with two limbs meeting or a muscle at its shortest. The earlier form of this rule said push versus pull, which covered the estate until adduction and convergence machines were added and did not describe them at all. Convergence in particular is not lockout: D6 Chest Press and D5 Arm Cross both travel toward the midline and differ only in that the press reaches extension. Both were checked on 24 October and they land on opposite sides.

defaultTargetTempo.note: Prescribed across the estate. Held here once rather than copied onto every machine, so changing the prescription is one edit. A machine's own targetTempo stays null unless it needs to differ — null means inherit this. Order is concentric first, which is how the app's inputs read; standard coaching notation starts with the eccentric, so 4-2-4-2 is only identical because it is symmetric.

unilateral: Machines that can be worked one side at a time. A side is recorded with the set so left and right stay separate: they are different work and averaging them hides the asymmetry that is worth seeing. The hold rules do not change with side.
maxStackTravelMm: Hard stop to hard stop: how far the carrier can travel on this machine, not how far any particular client moves it. A client's own range varies with their build and the seat setting, and the app does not need it in advance — it measures each set's stroke from that recording and judges on the spot whether the prescribed tempo is measurable through it. What a fixed per-machine number is good for is the two things a client's range cannot give: a ceiling, since any reading longer than the machine can travel is wrong whatever else is true, and a reference for checking the app's distances against a known length. Measure it with the phone mounted as in use, and note which part was taped and which part the phone travels on — a cable ratio between the stack and the carrier would make those two different numbers.
